pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Acid Reactions & Salts

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Chemical reactions):** pupils are taught "reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen" and "neutralisation of acids by alkalis, e.g. to produce a salt plus water," and to represent chemical reactions using word equations.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred — the salt formed is a new substance with new properties.

- **Operational details:** Build from the pupil's existing pH/neutralisation knowledge to the idea that neutralising an acid does not make the atoms vanish — it converts them into a NEW substance, a salt, plus water (or plus hydrogen when a metal is used). Anchor the two reaction families: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen (test the gas with a lit splint, the squeaky pop); acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation, follow with an indicator to pH 7). Teach the naming rule that the acid decides the salt's surname: hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate; the metal or the metal in the alkali gives the first name. Keep it to word equations at KS3 — symbol equations and mole calculations are KS4. Recover the salt by evaporating the solution to grow visible crystals, closing the loop that a dissolved product is still there.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child predicts the products of acid + metal and acid + alkali reactions and names the salt from the acid used, writing a correct word equation — without yet needing balanced symbol equations.
bestPractices: Anchor to the two canonical reaction families explicitly — acid + metal → salt + hydrogen, and acid + alkali → salt + water — and keep returning to them so pupils sort any new example into one or the other.

Make the salt-naming rule a predictable pattern the child applies, not a list to memorise: the acid fixes the ending (hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate), the metal fixes the first word.
Use the hydrogen pop-test and an indicator endpoint as observable signatures that distinguish the two families in real time.
Recover the salt by evaporation so the child sees the dissolved product is a real, tangible solid — reinforcing conservation of matter across the reaction.
Stay at word-equation level; defer symbol equations, state symbols and moles to KS4 so the productive naming rule is secure first.
keyRepresentations: The two family templates: 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen' and 'acid + alkali → salt + water'.
A word-equation builder that assembles reactants and products with the salt auto-named from the acid.
The pH/indicator scale used as a neutralisation endpoint (stops at 7).
The hydrogen squeaky-pop test as the gas signature.
Evaporating basin growing salt crystals as the recovered product.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking neutralisation makes the acid 'disappear' rather than converting it into a salt plus water.
Believing a salt means only table salt (sodium chloride), not a whole family of compounds.
Assuming every acid reaction gives off a gas — confusing acid + metal (hydrogen released) with acid + alkali (no gas, water formed).
Mixing up the salt endings, e.g. expecting sulfuric acid to give a 'sulfide' rather than a sulfate.
Thinking the dissolved salt is 'gone' once it is in solution, rather than recoverable by evaporation.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn that reacting an acid does not make matter vanish — atoms are rearranged into NEW substances: a salt plus water when the acid is neutralised by an alkali or a metal oxide/hydroxide, or a salt plus hydrogen when a reactive metal reacts. Learners anchor the reaction families (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen, shown with reactive metals such as magnesium, zinc or iron and dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid; acid + alkali → salt + water; acid + metal oxide or metal hydroxide → salt + water), apply a predictable salt-naming rule (the acid fixes the ending: hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate; the metal or metal-in-the-base gives the first word), observe family-distinguishing signatures (hydrogen squeaky-pop test; indicator reaching pH 7), and recover the dissolved salt by evaporation to crystals. Work stays at word-equation level; symbol equations, state symbols and moles are deferred. Activities are proposals; concrete bench chemistry and manipulable models are complementary ways to run the predict–observe–name loop.

activities.title: The salt maker: run reactions, name the salt, write the word equation
feedback: If a learner expects every acid reaction to give off a gas, contrast the two runs directly: a reactive metal in dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid fizzes and gives hydrogen (squeaky pop), while acid + alkali gives no gas and forms water — same acid, different partner, different products.
If a learner writes 'sulfide' for a sulfuric-acid salt, point back to the ending rule: sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate, hydrochloric→chloride.

If a learner thinks the neutral mixture holds 'nothing', have them evaporate it — the leftover crystals prove the salt was dissolved there all along; 'neutral' means acidity and alkalinity are balanced, not that matter disappeared.
Once three or four runs are done, ask the learner to predict the salt's name before any writing appears, confirming the rule is felt rather than looked up.
activities.rationale: The topic is a set of rule-governed transformations: pick reactants, run the reaction, observe products, name the salt. Letting learners choose reactants and see the fizz / pop-test / indicator endpoint makes the naming rule felt through repetition, and the evaporation step makes it tangible that the products did not vanish (the dissolved salt is recovered, although the water driven off is lost, so evaporation does not itself demonstrate mass conservation). Optional interactive affordances (dragging reactants into a flask, a splint giving a pop, an indicator sweeping colour to pH 7, an auto-assembled word equation, an evaporate-to-crystals step) make the learning mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not required.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen, and neutralisation of acids by alkalis to produce a salt plus water, using word equations.

Salt naming follows the acid: hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates; acids react with metals to give salt + hydrogen and with alkalis to give salt + water.
learnerActions: Choose dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid and pair it with a moderately reactive metal such as magnesium, zinc or iron (not copper, which does not react, and never sodium or potassium); observe bubbles rising and test the gas at the mouth of the tube with a lit splint — a squeaky pop signals hydrogen. (Nitric acid is fine for the naming rule with alkalis and oxides, but with metals it usually gives nitrogen oxides rather than hydrogen, so it is not used for this run.)

Keep the same acid but this time use an alkali (e.g. sodium hydroxide solution) instead of the metal; with indicator already in the acid, add the alkali gradually, a little at a time — observe that there is no fizz, and watch the indicator change until it shows pH 7 (neutralisation), giving salt + water.

After each run, state the salt's full name before it is written out, deriving the surname from the acid (chloride/sulfate/nitrate) and the first word from the metal or the metal in the alkali, then write the complete word equation (e.g. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen).

Finish by evaporating the neutral solution to drive off the water and leave visible salt crystals in the dish (for purer crystals, repeat the neutralisation with the same volumes but no indicator, because indicator left in the solution colours the salt).

Repeat with new pairings — acid/reactive metal (dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid), acid/alkali, and acid/metal oxide or hydroxide (e.g. copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water) — so the naming rule generalises across examples rather than being memorised as a list.
activities.intendedInsight: Neutralising or reacting an acid converts it into a real, recoverable salt (plus hydrogen or water) — matter is conserved and rearranged, not destroyed — and the salt's name follows predictably from the acid and the metal.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: what is left when the water evaporates?
feedback: If the learner predicts an empty dish, treat that prediction as the diagnostic: the crystals that appear show matter remained — reframe 'neutral' as balanced acidity/alkalinity, not annihilation.

Full-credit reasoning names salt + water as the products and explicitly rejects 'cancelled to nothing'; a partial answer rejects 'nothing' but cannot yet name the specific salt for a new acid/base pair.
Probe generalisation: hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide gives potassium chloride, not sodium chloride — the first name comes from the metal in the alkali used.
activities.rationale: Eliciting a pre-observation prediction about the products is the diagnostic that separates a learner who tracks conservation of matter from one who reads 'neutral' as things disappearing. The written prediction must come before the observation so the reasoning, not just the outcome, is assessed.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen, and neutralisation of acids by alkalis to produce a salt plus water, using word equations.
Students analyse and interpret data on properties of substances before and after they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Neutralise an acid with an alkali until the indicator reads pH 7.
BEFORE evaporating, write down a prediction: if all the water is driven off, what (if anything) will remain, and WHY?
Evaporate the water and compare the result with the prediction.
Write the word equation for what happened (acid + alkali → salt + water) and explain in words why 'neutral' does not mean 'empty'.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'cancelled to nothing' model predicts an empty dish; the solid salt crystals that remain disprove it. Neutralisation produces a salt plus water, and mass is conserved as atoms rearrange into new products.

activities.title: Complete and name: word-equation practice across families
feedback: For 'sulfuric acid + zinc', the correct completion is 'zinc sulfate + hydrogen'; if a learner writes 'zinc sulfide', return to the sulfuric→sulfate ending.

If a learner answers 'salt + water' for an acid + metal reaction, re-anchor the squeaky-pop test: reactive metals in dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid release hydrogen, whereas alkalis, metal oxides and metal hydroxides form water.
Treat 'salt' as a whole family of compounds (copper sulfate, potassium nitrate, …), not only edible table salt; the specific salt depends on the acid and base used.
activities.rationale: Completing equations, matching endings, choosing the gas, and naming salts for new pairs exercise the productive rule rather than mere recognition. Constructing the full equation and the salt name — not just picking from options — is what demonstrates the generalisation. A related prerequisite on acid+metal products can be revisited if hydrogen is persistently omitted.
sourceClaims: Salt naming follows the acid: hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates; acids react with metals to give salt + hydrogen and with alkalis to give salt + water.
KS3 pupils are taught reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen, and neutralisation of acids by alkalis to produce a salt plus water, using word equations.
learnerActions: Complete partial word equations, e.g. 'sulfuric acid + zinc → zinc ____ + ____', filling both the salt surname and the gas.
Match each acid to its salt ending: hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate.
Decide, for a given pairing, whether hydrogen or water is produced, and justify the choice by naming the family (acid+reactive metal vs acid+alkali or acid+metal oxide/hydroxide).
Name the salt from an unfamiliar acid/base pair (e.g. hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide → potassium chloride + water) and state why it is not sodium chloride.
State the pH at the neutralisation endpoint (7) and name the gas test for hydrogen (lit splint, squeaky pop).
activities.intendedInsight: The productive salt-naming rule and the family distinction (hydrogen vs water) can be applied to new pairings, not just recognised in familiar ones.

activities.title: Vocabulary and family contrast (introductory scaffold)
feedback: Use this to establish terms, then move to running varied pairings — a fixed picture introduces vocabulary but does not let the learner change reactants or feel the naming rule generalise, so follow it with the salt-maker and equation-completion activities.
Check understanding by asking the learner to produce (not just recognise) one word equation from each family after studying the diagram.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram with reveal-on-tap parts can introduce vocabulary and contrast the two families efficiently, but it is a scaffold: it cannot let the child vary reactants, observe the gas test, or construct and name salts independently, which is the heart of the topic.
learnerActions: Study a labelled picture of a neutralisation (acid + alkali → salt + water), revealing the names of the acid, the alkali, the salt crystals and the role of each part.
Contrast a side-by-side pair of the two reaction families and say, for each, whether a gas is released and what the other product is.
Connect the vocabulary to a real application: indigestion tablets neutralise stomach acid, and treating acidic soil raises its pH.
activities.intendedInsight: Names and family vocabulary (acid, alkali, salt, neutralisation, hydrogen) and the two product patterns are introduced before learners run and generalise them.

constraints: Stay at word-equation level; defer symbol equations, state symbols, balancing and mole calculations to the next stage (KS4).

The labelled-diagram activity is an introductory scaffold: it builds vocabulary but does not elicit independent construction of equations or salt names, so it must be followed by activities where learners run reactions and name salts themselves.

Keep returning to the canonical templates (acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen, using dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid; acid + alkali → salt + water) and include acid + metal oxide or metal hydroxide → salt + water as a required third route, because the objective covers metal oxides/hydroxides; sort each new example into one of these families.
Screen or app models of the reactions are complements to, not substitutes for, a real bench neutralisation and evaporation done in class; pair the simulated loop with hands-on practical work.

Recognition-only tasks (matching, multiple choice) check the rule but do not by themselves show the learner can independently construct a correct word equation or name a salt for a new pairing — include construction tasks.
Teach 'salt' as a general class of acid+base products; do not let examples imply every neutralisation yields edible table salt.
In the neutralisation step, the alkali (or acid) is added gradually with indicator already present to reach pH 7; the indicator only reports pH and does not itself drive the reaction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.
The original row listed two sources as not verified (NGSS MS-PS1-2 and the RSC making-salts resource); their claims are reused here as teaching principles, not as verified evidence.

Self-audit of chemistry: 'sulfuric acid + zinc → zinc sulfate + hydrogen' is correct (sulfate, not sulfide; hydrogen gas, not water). Acid+metal releases hydrogen; acid+alkali forms water; acid+metal oxide/hydroxide forms water — these product sets are distinct and were kept distinct. The salt's first name derives from the metal (or the metal in the alkali): hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide gives potassium chloride, not sodium chloride. No arithmetic or force/motion content required checking here.

Fixed a sequencing incoherence in the salt-maker neutralisation step: the alkali is now added gradually once, with the indicator already present in the acid, so the learner observes both the absence of fizz and the indicator sweep to pH 7; the indicator reports pH and does not drive the reaction.

The original 'poor fit' rationales asserting that a 3D lab 'adds nothing' and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' the loop were softened: these are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the sources. The genuine, retained limit is that recognition-only formats do not elicit independent construction and that a static diagram cannot let learners vary reactants.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: neutralise acid with alkali to pH 7, then ask the child to predict what remains if the water is evaporated away, and WHY, before doing it. A 'cancelled to nothing' model predicts an empty dish. Evaporation leaves solid salt crystals. The pre-observation reasoning about products is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I evaporate the neutral mixture, what would I find — and what does that prove about 'cancelling to nothing'?
Indigestion tablets work by neutralising stomach acid. What's being made in your stomach when they work?
Hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide — name the salt. Why isn't it sodium chloride?
How is the acid+metal reaction different in its products from acid+alkali? What test proves it?
assess.correctAnswer: No — nothing vanished. Neutralisation produces a SALT plus WATER: here sodium chloride dissolved in water (acid + alkali → salt + water). 'Neutral' means the acidity and alkalinity are balanced, not that matter disappeared — the atoms rearranged into new products (mass is conserved). Full marks name salt + water as the products and reject 'cancelled to nothing'.

errorPatterns.pattern: neutralisation makes the substances disappear / cancel to nothing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaporate the neutral mixture — solid salt is left behind, proving matter remained. Reframe 'neutral' as balanced, not empty; write acid + alkali → salt + water.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing — the acid and alkali cancelled each other out completely.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the beaker holds 'nothing' or 'just cancelled out' after neutralising

errorPatterns.pattern: 'salt' means only table salt (NaCl), not a general class of compounds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce 'salt' as the whole family of acid+base products; the specific salt depends on the acid and base used. Table salt is just one member.
errorPatterns.distractor: It makes table salt you could eat, whatever acid and alkali you use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects edible table salt from every neutralisation, or is confused when the salt is copper sulfate/potassium nitrate

errorPatterns.pattern: acid + metal gives the same products as acid + alkali (misremembers hydrogen vs water)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the three routes: acid+metal → salt + HYDROGEN; acid+alkali → salt + water; acid+metal oxide → salt + water. Use the squeaky-pop test to anchor hydrogen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: writes 'salt + water' for acid+metal, or omits the hydrogen gas

responseLevels.gap: Says neutralisation leaves 'nothing'/cancels out; thinks 'salt' only means table salt; muddles the product sets.
responseLevels.full: Names salt + water as neutralisation products, treats 'salt' as a general class and names the specific salt from the acid/base used, distinguishes all three acid-reaction routes with their gas/water products, and grounds it in conservation of mass and a real application.
responseLevels.partial: States acid+alkali → salt + water and rejects 'nothing', but can't name the specific salt for a new acid/base pair or distinguish acid+metal (hydrogen) from acid+alkali (water) — the pattern without generalisation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I mix hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide (an alkali) in the right amounts and the mixture ends up neutral, pH 7. A student says 'so now there's nothing left — they cancelled each other out to nothing.' Is that right — what is actually in the beaker now? Then explain what neutralisation really produces.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two question distinguishes a child who tracks the products of neutralisation (a salt + water form; matter conserved) from one who reads 'neutral' as annihilation. It also probes whether 'salt' is understood as a general class (any acid+base salt) rather than only table salt.
